pos: n. phrase (biblical and practical theology; the discipline of honest, faith-saturated grief addressed to God, grounded in the Psalms and the prophetic tradition)
etymology: Lament from Latin lamentum (wailing, moaning), related to lamīna (thin metal plate, the idea of beating one's chest). Theology from Greek theos (God) + logos (word, reason). Lament theology names not merely the act of weeping but the disciplined, structured address of honest grief to God — grief that does not abandon faith but wrestles within it, as Jacob wrestled and received the blessing.
biblical_def: Lament theology is the biblical discipline of bringing unvarnished grief, suffering, confusion, and protest before God in faith-saturated prayer, trusting that He is sovereign, present, and worthy to receive honest address. The Psalter is the primary classroom: roughly one-third of the 150 Psalms are lament Psalms, and the genre spans the full spectrum from communal sorrow (Ps 44; 74; 80) to individual anguish (Ps 22; 88; 130). Psalm 22:1 — “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” — is the paradigmatic lament: utter desolation addressed to the God who is still “my God.” Jesus cried this from the cross (Matt 27:46), sanctifying lament as the proper language of the Son in His deepest suffering. Psalm 88 is noteworthy as the only Psalm that ends without resolution — it closes in darkness, demonstrating that lament before God does not require forced positivity or a tidy doxology. Lamentations anchors the discipline in corporate grief: Jeremiah weeps over Jerusalem's fall with unsparing honesty while clinging to the steadfastness of God's mercies (Lam 3:22–23). The Reformed tradition (Calvin, Spurgeon, Martyn Lloyd-Jones) insists that honest lament is not faithlessness but a form of trust: only those who believe God is real and sovereign bring their grief to Him rather than suppressing it or directing it at His absence. Lament theology is thus the antidote to both the stoic suppression of grief and the prosperity gospel's denial of it.
webster_summary: The biblical and theological discipline of addressing honest, faith-saturated grief to God; grounded in the Psalms of lament, the book of Lamentations, and the prophetic tradition — and sanctified by Christ's own lament from the cross.
webster_full: LAMENT THEOLOGY, n. phrase. The branch of biblical and practical theology that studies, recovers, and commends the practice of directed, honest grief addressed to God — as distinct from stoic suppression, therapeutic venting, or faithless despair. The Psalter is the primary source: approximately fifty of the 150 Psalms are classified as individual or communal laments, making grief-prayer the most common genre in the Bible's inspired prayer book.

The structure of a biblical lament follows a recognizable pattern: an address to God, a complaint or protest about present suffering, a petition for deliverance, an expression of trust, and frequently a vow of praise. Psalm 22 models the full movement: from “Why have You forsaken me?” to “For He has not despised nor scorned the suffering of the afflicted one.” The movement is not required to resolve — Psalm 88 ends in darkness — but it remains addressed to God throughout.

Calvin's commentary on the Psalms treats the Psalter as an anatomy of the soul; his reading of the lament Psalms insists on their literal, historical weight — not as mere pious exercises but as the actual cries of actual sufferers which the Holy Spirit preserved because the church would need them in every generation. This Reformed instinct resists the allegorizing that drains the laments of their concrete anguish.

The book of Job provides the most extended biblical instance of lament theology: Job's three friends model the false comfort of systematic theology wielded against a suffering man, while God's commendation of Job over his friends (42:7) vindicates honest, argued lament over pious platitude. The church needs both the theology and the permission — permission to say it hurts without being told the confession means weak faith.

Lamentations 3:22–23 demonstrates the Reformed resolution: the steadfastness of the LORD's mercies is the reason for hope, not the cessation of suffering. Lament theology is thus not pessimism; it is realism held within covenant: the God who permits the suffering is the God who promised to see us through it.

corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel evacuates lament from Christian worship by treating suffering as evidence of weak faith, while therapeutic Christianity domesticates lament by redirecting it from God to a counselor — both rob the believer of the Psalter's most formative discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel, in its various forms — Word of Faith, health-and-wealth, and its softer evangelical iterations — treats suffering as abnormal and largely avoidable for the properly faithful believer. On this account, lament is at best a transitional cry on the way to claiming a promised victory; prolonged lament signals a faith deficiency to be corrected by more positive confession. This reading systematically suppresses the Psalter's most common genre. It cannot account for Psalm 88, which ends in darkness without resolution, or for Habakkuk's sustained complaint, or for Christ's cry of dereliction from the cross. A Christianity that cannot lament is not the Christianity of Scripture; it is a religious performance that abandons the sufferer at precisely the moment the Psalter has the most to say.

Therapeutic Christianity, on the other hand, displaces lament from its proper address to God and routes it instead to the therapist's couch, the support group, or the “safe space.” This is not without value at the pastoral level, but when it replaces rather than supplements the practice of prayer-lament, it severs the grief from its proper object. Lament theology insists that the God who ordained the suffering is the God who must receive the complaint about it — and that He is large enough to handle honest protest. The Psalms were not given to the therapist but to the congregation, to be prayed and sung together as the covenant community brings its corporate weight of sorrow before the Throne.
roots_summary: Lament theology is rooted in the Psalter, Lamentations, Job, and the prophetic tradition, developed in Calvin's Psalms commentary and Puritan pastoral theology, and recovered for modern evangelical use by theologians such as Walter Brueggemann and Dan Allender.
roots_lines: Psalter lament genre (approximately 50 Psalms) — the most common literary form in the Bible's prayer book; the Psalms of individual lament (22, 42, 88, 130) and communal lament (44, 74, 80, 137) form the backbone of biblical prayer-grief.

Book of Job — the extended test case of lament theology; God commends Job's honest protest over his friends' pious platitudes (Job 42:7), establishing that argued, directed lament is more honoring to God than systematic comfort wielded against a sufferer.

Book of Lamentations — Jeremiah's five-poem dirge over Jerusalem's fall; the supreme instance of corporate lament in Scripture, combining unsparing honesty about national catastrophe with the anchor of covenant steadfastness (3:22–23).

Calvin, Commentary on the Psalms (1557) — the Reformed locus classicus; Calvin reads the lament Psalms as the Holy Spirit's provision for the church in every generation of suffering, insisting that the God who gave these words is the God who invites them.

Walter Brueggemann, The Message of the Psalms (1984) / Dan Allender, The Cry of the Soul (1994) — modern Reformed-adjacent recoveries of lament as a spiritual discipline; to be read critically but recognized as part of the late-twentieth-century recovery of a suppressed biblical genre.
usage: Psalm 88 ends in darkness — “darkness is my closest friend” — without resolution or doxology; this is not a failed Psalm but a gift to every believer whose suffering has not resolved neatly, demonstrating that honest lament addressed to God is itself a form of faith.

Pastors who train their congregations to lament are protecting them against both the false comfort of the prosperity gospel and the false silence of stoic Christianity: the Psalms provide exactly the language believers need for grief, and the congregation that sings them together discovers it is not alone.

Jesus' quotation of Psalm 22:1 from the cross (Matt 27:46) permanently canonizes the lament Psalm as Christologically significant — the Son of God prayed the lament of a forsaken Israelite, sanctifying the form and assuring every believer who prays it that they pray it in company with their Savior.

pos: n. phrase (practical and ascetical theology; the deliberate shaping of a believer's soul toward Christlikeness through the Spirit's work in the ordinary means of grace)
etymology: Spiritual from Latin spiritualis, from spiritus (breath, Spirit); relating to the Holy Spirit's work and the immaterial dimension of human life. Formation from Latin formatio — formare (to form, shape) — the act of being given a definite shape or character. In the classical theological sense, spiritual formation names what God does to the believer through the Spirit by means of Word, prayer, and sacrament: He forms Christ in them (Gal 4:19), working the image of the Son into every dimension of the soul.
biblical_def: Spiritual formation — in its biblical sense — is the Spirit's work of conforming the believer progressively to the image of Christ through the ordinary means of grace: the Word preached and read, prayer, the Lord's Supper, baptism, fellowship, and suffering. The Apostle Paul names the goal: “Him we proclaim — admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom — so that we may present every person mature in Christ” (Col 1:28). The means is not technique but the Spirit who uses His appointed instruments. Paul's labor-pain metaphor in Galatians 4:19 — “until Christ is formed in you” — describes the apostolic investment in the church's formation: it is agonizing, personal, patient, and directed toward a Person (Christ), not a set of spiritual competencies. Philippians 2:12–13 holds the active and passive together: “work out your salvation with fear and trembling — for it is God who is at work in you both to will and to work for His good pleasure.” The believer's effort (the means) and God's sovereign operation (the efficient cause) are not competitors but co-operating realities. Hebrews 12:14 adds the ecclesial horizon: “pursue the sanctification without which no one will see the Lord.” Spiritual formation in the Reformed sense is therefore always Word-and-Spirit driven, means-of-grace-centered, and directed toward visible holiness within the covenant community — never private mysticism or self-designed technique.
webster_summary: The Spirit's progressive work of conforming the believer to the image of Christ through the ordinary means of grace — Word, prayer, sacrament, and suffering — as distinct from self-designed spiritual technique or contemplative mysticism borrowed from Catholic ascetical tradition.
webster_full: SPIRITUAL FORMATION, n. phrase. The process by which a believer is shaped into the likeness of Christ through the Holy Spirit's work in and through the ordinary means of grace. The biblical language is “formed” (Gal 4:19, morphoo — given the definitive shape of Christ within the soul), “conformed” (Rom 8:29, summorphos — bearing together the same form as), and “transformed” (Rom 12:2, metamorphoo — the ongoing renewal of the mind). All three Greek terms point to the Spirit's active shaping work, not to techniques the believer masters.

The Reformed tradition grounds spiritual formation in the means of grace, not in spiritual exercises developed apart from them. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 154) names the outward means: the Word (read, preached, and heard), the sacraments, and prayer — these are the ordinary channels through which the Spirit works. The extraordinary and the self-designed are suspect; the ordinary and the appointed are sufficient.

The Puritan tradition produced the richest practical literature of Reformed spiritual formation: John Owen's On the Mortification of Sin (1656), Thomas Watson's A Body of Practical Divinity (1692), and Richard Baxter's The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650) expose the inner life, name the Spirit's instruments, and resist any shortcut that bypasses the Word. This is the model — not the contemplative exercises of Ignatius Loyola or the centering-prayer tradition of Thomas Merton.

Galatians 4:19 gives the goal and the agent: Paul travails in birth pains “until Christ is formed in you.” The goal is not spiritual wellness, emotional health, or a generic flourishing; it is Christ — the Person, the character, the obedience — reproduced in every dimension of the believer's life by the Spirit through the Word.

Philippians 2:12–13 supplies the pattern for the believer's active role: “work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you.” The divine sovereignty does not produce passivity; it produces strenuous, humble, reverent activity directed at holiness — which is exactly what the Puritan tradition called “practical religion.”

corruption_summary: The modern “spiritual formation movement” — driven by Richard Foster's Celebration of Discipline and Dallas Willard's works — has imported Catholic contemplative practices (centering prayer, lectio divina as mystical technique, solitude exercises) into evangelical churches in place of the Word-and-Spirit ordinary means of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Richard Foster's Celebration of Discipline (1978) became the generative text of the modern spiritual formation movement in evangelicalism and drew heavily on medieval Catholic mysticism — Thomas à Kempis, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross, and Thomas Merton — to construct a set of “spiritual disciplines” presented as the universal Christian path to formation. Dallas Willard's The Spirit of the Disciplines (1988) and Renovation of the Heart (2002) gave the movement its theoretical architecture. While both authors contain useful material on practice and intentionality, the movement as a whole has tended to substitute contemplative technique — particularly “centering prayer,” a practice derived from Basil Pennington's reading of Merton and the Desert Fathers — for the means of grace appointed by Christ in Scripture. Centering prayer's method of emptying the mind of all content to receive God's presence is incompatible with biblical prayer, which is addressed, specific, and saturated with the Word.

The deeper problem of the spiritual formation movement is methodological: it treats formation as something the believer achieves through selected practices rather than something the Spirit works through appointed means. This is not the Reformed distinction between means and end; it is a subtle synergism of technique. The Reformers and Puritans were not opposed to discipline — they were the most disciplined practitioners of Word-saturated daily life in Christian history — but they located the formative power in the Word preached and the Spirit who uses it, not in techniques borrowed from sources the Reformers deliberately corrected. Reformation-and-beyond spiritual formation is: preach the Word, pray the Psalms, take the Lord's Supper, mortify the flesh, and wait on the God who forms His people through His own appointed means.
roots_summary: Spiritual formation in the biblical sense is rooted in the Pauline formation language (Gal 4:19; Rom 8:29; 12:2), the Westminster means-of-grace theology, the Puritan practical divinity tradition, and the 1689 LBCF's account of the Spirit's work in sanctification.
roots_lines: Galatians 4:19 / Romans 8:29 / Romans 12:2 — the three Pauline formation terms (morphoo, summorphos, metamorphoo); all three locate the formative agency in God's Spirit shaping the believer into the image of the Son, not in the believer's technique.

Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 154–158 — the appointed means of grace (Word, sacraments, prayer) as the ordinary channels of the Spirit's formative work; the catechism's account is the best Reformed summary of the mechanics of spiritual formation.

John Owen, On the Mortification of Sin (1656) — the Puritan practical-formation masterwork; Owen's central axiom — “Be killing sin or it will be killing you” — epitomizes the active-yet-Spirit-dependent character of Reformed formation.

Thomas Watson, A Body of Practical Divinity (1692) / Richard Baxter, The Reformed Pastor (1656) — the corporate dimension of Reformed formation: the pastor's role in shaping the congregation through preaching, catechizing, and personal pastoral care.

1689 LBCF, Chapter 13 (Of Sanctification) — the confession's account of progressive, Spirit-wrought, Word-saturated sanctification as the Reformed framework for understanding what spiritual formation is and is not.
usage: When a church adopts a “spiritual formation curriculum” built around centering prayer and contemplative silence, it has replaced the Reformed means of grace with Catholic ascetical technique; the corrective is not to abandon intentionality in discipleship but to reground it in the Word preached, the Psalms prayed, and the Supper taken.

Galatians 4:19 reveals that spiritual formation is apostolic labor, not self-improvement: Paul is in labor pains until Christ is formed in the Galatians, meaning formation is a pastoral investment that requires the Word proclaimed and applied — not a personal retreat to a monastery.

The danger of the formation movement is not emphasis on discipline (the Puritans out-disciplined anyone) but the source of the disciplines: practices derived from Catholic mysticism carry assumptions about the nature of God's presence and the role of the mind in prayer that are incompatible with the Protestant sola Scriptura framework.

pos: n. phrase (eschatological position; the view that the majority of New Testament prophecy — including the Olivet Discourse and most of Revelation — was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, while the Second Coming and Final Resurrection remain future)
etymology: Partial from Latin partialis, from pars (part); indicating that only part of the prophetic material is held to have been fulfilled, as distinct from full or hyper-preterism. Preterism from Latin praeteritus (past), from praeterire (to go past, pass by); the view that the events prophesied have already passed. The “partial” qualifier distinguishes this position from full preterism (which holds even the Resurrection and Second Coming to be past events), which Reformed confessional theology unanimously rejects as outside the bounds of orthodoxy.
biblical_def: Partial preterism is the eschatological interpretation that holds that the bulk of New Testament prophecy — particularly the Olivet Discourse of Matthew 24, Mark 13, and Luke 21, and the greater part of the book of Revelation — was fulfilled in and around the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. Matthew 24:34 is the interpretive pivot: “Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” Partial preterists read “this generation” as referring to the first-century Jewish generation, making the fulfillment of most of Matthew 24:4–34 events of the years AD 66–70. Revelation 1:1 supports this: “the things that must shortly take place” — and Revelation 1:3 adds: “for the time is near.” Partial preterism reads these temporal markers as genuine first-century time references, not timeless or symbolic. Distinguished from full (or hyper-) preterism, partial preterism affirms that the physical, bodily Second Coming of Christ, the bodily resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment remain as future literal events — thus remaining within the bounds of Nicene orthodoxy. Major partial preterist voices in the Reformed tradition include R.C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus), Kenneth Gentry, and Gary DeMar. The Westminster Confession and 1689 LBCF are eschatologically flexible on this question; partial preterism is a legitimate position within the confessional Reformed tradition.
webster_summary: The eschatological view that most New Testament prophecy — especially the Olivet Discourse and most of Revelation — was fulfilled in the AD 70 destruction of Jerusalem, while the Second Coming, Resurrection, and Final Judgment remain as future, literal events; a legitimate position within confessional Reformed eschatology.
webster_full: PARTIAL PRETERISM, n. phrase. The interpretation of New Testament prophecy that places the fulfillment of most prophetic material in the first century AD — specifically, in the events surrounding the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in AD 70 — while retaining the bodily Second Coming, bodily Resurrection of the dead, and Final Judgment as future literal events. The “partial” qualifier is essential: it distinguishes this position from full preterism, which denies any future eschatological events, and which Reformed confessional theology uniformly rejects.

Matthew 24:34 (“this generation will not pass away until all these things take place”) and Revelation 1:1, 3 (“things which must shortly take place”; “the time is near”) are the textual anchors. Partial preterists read these temporal markers as genuine first-century time references: Jesus was predicting the fall of Jerusalem within the lifetime of His hearers, and John was writing to seven first-century churches about events imminently approaching them. The alternative — that “shortly” and “near” mean 2,000+ years hence — requires hermeneutical gymnastics that partial preterism argues are unnecessary.

The major literary case for partial preterism in the modern Reformed world is R.C. Sproul's The Last Days According to Jesus (1998), which argues from the time-text evidence that the “last days” language of the New Testament refers to the last days of the Old Covenant economy — the period from Christ's ascension to the Temple's destruction. Kenneth Gentry's Before Jerusalem Fell (1989) argues for an early date of Revelation (pre-AD 70) to support the same conclusion.

Partial preterism is compatible with amillennialism (which it most naturally pairs with), with postmillennialism (with some adjustment), and with certain historic premillennial readings. It is not compatible with classical dispensationalism, which requires the majority of Revelation's events to be future. The 1689 LBCF and Westminster Confession do not specify among these options, making partial preterism a legitimate intra-confessional position.

Full or hyper-preterism (which holds the Second Coming and Resurrection to have already occurred spiritually in AD 70) is outside the bounds of orthodox Christianity; it denies the Apostles' Creed's “He shall come again to judge the living and the dead.” No confessional Reformed body accepts full preterism as within the pale.

corruption_summary: Full or hyper-preterism extends partial preterism's first-century fulfillment to include the Second Coming and Resurrection, placing these events in AD 70 and thus departing from every historic creed and confession; meanwhile, popularized dispensationalism misreads “this generation” as a reference to a future generation that sees the signs, contorting the natural meaning of the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Full preterism — associated with Max King, Don Preston, and the Covenant Eschatology movement — extends the preterist logic to its terminus: if most prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, then the Second Coming and Resurrection must have occurred spiritually in AD 70 as well. This conclusion is incompatible with every historic Christian creed. The Apostles' Creed affirms: “He will come again to judge the living and the dead.” The Nicene Creed: “He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and His kingdom will have no end.” The 1689 LBCF (32–33) affirms a bodily resurrection and a future final judgment. Full preterism is not a legitimate option within confessional Christianity, regardless of its hermeneutical energy. No Reformed denomination accepts it.

Dispensational popular eschatology takes the opposite error: reading “this generation” in Matthew 24:34 as a reference to a future generation that witnesses the signs of the Great Tribulation (signs that dispensationalism places entirely in a seven-year period preceding Christ's return). This requires the word “generation” (genea) to mean something it never means elsewhere in Matthew (where it consistently refers to the contemporaries of Jesus — e.g., Matt 11:16; 12:39, 41, 42, 45; 23:36). The dispensational reading protects a future-fulfillment scheme at the cost of natural exegesis; partial preterism reads the text straightforwardly and allows the time texts to mean what they say.
roots_summary: Partial preterism traces to the early church (Eusebius), was given its modern Reformed articulation by Moses Stuart, and has been recovered by R.C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry, and Gary DeMar as a serious exegetical alternative within the confessional Reformed tradition.
roots_lines: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History (c. AD 313) — the earliest sustained reading of Matthew 24 as fulfilled in the AD 70 siege; Eusebius reads the Olivet Discourse as a detailed prophecy of the events Josephus records in The Jewish War.

Moses Stuart, Commentary on the Apocalypse (1845) — the nineteenth-century American scholarly recovery of preterist exegesis; Stuart's work laid the exegetical groundwork for later Reformed preterist readings.

R.C. Sproul, The Last Days According to Jesus (1998) — the most accessible modern Reformed case; Sproul argues that the time-text evidence is so strong that any honest reading of Matthew 24 must take the first-century fulfillment seriously.

Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell (1989) — the technical argument for a pre-AD 70 date of Revelation; if Revelation was written under Nero, its “imminent” language refers to events that were, from the author's perspective, genuinely near.

1689 LBCF, Chapters 32–33 (Of the State of Man after Death / Of the Last Judgment) — the confessional limits: bodily resurrection of all the dead, a final judgment of all persons, and the eternal states of heaven and hell; these remain future and literal on every orthodox eschatological reading.
usage: Partial preterism does not deny the Second Coming or Final Judgment; it relocates most of Matthew 24 to the past, which actually clarifies the future hope — the return of Christ is no longer mixed up with first-century siege language but stands distinct as a future, glorious, unconditioned event.

The strongest argument for partial preterism is the simplest: Jesus said “this generation” would see all these things, and “this generation” in every other use in Matthew means the contemporaries of Jesus — the burden of proof falls on those who give it any other meaning.

Pastors should distinguish partial preterism from full preterism clearly: the former is within the confessional Reformed tradition and deserves a fair hearing; the latter denies the bodily return of Christ and the future bodily resurrection and falls outside the bounds of historic Christian orthodoxy.

pos: n. phrase (sacramental theology; the practice of admitting baptized infants and young children to the Lord's Supper prior to any formal profession of faith)
etymology: Paedo- from Greek pais (child, infant). Communion from Latin communio (sharing, fellowship), from communis (common). The compound term names the liturgical practice of extending the Lord's Supper to covenant children who have been baptized but have not yet made a credible profession of faith. It is distinct from credobaptist practice, which requires conversion before any sacramental participation, and from the majority paedobaptist position, which requires a credible profession before the Supper even when baptism was administered in infancy.
biblical_def: Paedo-communion is the position that covenant children who have received baptism as infants should also be admitted to the Lord's Supper without waiting for a formal profession of faith. Its primary argument is covenantal consistency: if covenant infants receive the initiatory sign (baptism) on the strength of their parents' faith and their membership in the covenant community, why should they be excluded from the covenant meal? Proponents cite the Passover typology (Exo 12:26; Deut 16:11, 14), in which children clearly participated in the Old Testament feast that the Lord's Supper fulfills. The Sinai covenant included children in its covenant meals (Exo 24:11); New Covenant exclusion of children from the New Covenant meal therefore requires positive warrant from the New Testament. Against paedo-communion, the classic Protestant and Reformed position reads 1 Corinthians 11:28 — “a man must examine himself” — as establishing a cognitive and moral self-examination prerequisite that infants and young children cannot perform. The judgment warning of 1 Corinthians 11:29 (“he who eats and drinks, eats and drinks judgment to himself if he does not judge the body rightly”) makes responsible discernment a prerequisite for participation. The 1689 LBCF (30.3–4) and Westminster Standards require that communicants “examine themselves as to their knowledge to discern the Lord's body, their faith to feed upon him, their repentance, love, and new obedience” — a standard that excludes non-professing infants by design.
webster_summary: The sacramental practice of admitting baptized covenant infants and young children to the Lord's Supper prior to a credible profession of faith; argued on the basis of covenantal consistency with the Passover typology, but rejected by the Reformed and Baptist confessional standards on the basis of 1 Corinthians 11:28–29's self-examination requirement.
webster_full: PAEDO-COMMUNION, n. phrase. The practice of admitting baptized children, including infants, to the Lord's Supper on the basis of their covenant membership rather than requiring a personal profession of faith and self-examination. The position is advocated within certain Reformed, Federal Vision, and sacramental-covenantal communities, and is the norm in Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism (which administers Communion only at the age of reason, but some Orthodox traditions give it to all the baptized from infancy).

The paedo-communion argument proceeds from the Passover typology: the Passover meal, which the Lord's Supper fulfills and replaces (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 5:7), was a household feast from which children were not excluded. Exodus 12:26 assumes children will ask about it: “And it will come about when your children will say to you, 'What does this rite mean to you?'” Psalm 78:4 demonstrates that covenant children were included in the covenant community's memorial celebration: “We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD.” If the type included children, the argument runs, the antitype should not exclude them.

The classical Reformed and Baptist response is grounded in 1 Corinthians 11:27–32: Paul's warning that eating and drinking “in an unworthy manner” incurs judgment, combined with the command to “examine himself” before participating, establishes a cognitive and moral prerequisite that infants and non-professing young children cannot fulfill. The self-examination of verse 28 is not mere ritual; it requires faith, repentance, discernment of the Lord's body, and gratitude — capacities that require regenerate understanding. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 171–175) and the 1689 LBCF (30.3–4) codify this requirement.

The Federal Vision movement (Auburn Avenue Theology, Norman Shepherd, Peter Leithart) incorporated paedo-communion as a corollary of its covenantal theology, arguing that baptism confers a “real but resistible” covenant grace that entitles the baptized to full sacramental participation. This view was censured by multiple Reformed denominations (PCA, OPC, URCNA) as incompatible with the Westminster Standards' doctrine of saving grace and the nature of the Lord's Supper.

The majority confessional Reformed and Baptist position is that the Lord's Supper requires a credible profession of faith, demonstrated repentance, and the ability to self-examine — a standard that children reach at the age of a genuine profession, however young that may be. Early profession with genuine evidences is not delayed; it is welcomed. Perpetual exclusion of professing children is not the standard; non-professing children are not yet ready for the Table.

But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
1 Corinthians 11:29
